rationale: Start with a broad, mid-temperature scouting gradient to spread unknown compounds across the run while giving strong enough elution to observe all 10 if possible. This first run should reveal whether the sample is generally early-, late-, or broadly eluting and guide subsequent narrowing of the gradient window.

All 10 compounds eluted with perfect resolution, so the main opportunity is to reduce analysis time by shifting the gradient stronger at the start while keeping the same general slope and temperature. Raising phi0 should move the whole pattern earlier and test how much runtime can be cut before resolution begins to degrade.

Resolution is still comfortably perfect, so push the start composition one more step stronger to further compress the chromatogram and improve the time term. The closest pair remains well separated, making this a low-risk speed optimization.

The drop at phi0 0.25 shows the front pair is too compressed, so return to phi0 0.20 and shorten tG slightly to seek a better time term without sacrificing resolution. This tests whether modestly steeper gradients can beat the current best while keeping the early region under control.

The 18 min gradient retained full resolution and greatly improved CRF, so the next logical step is to shorten tG again to see if more time can be removed before the closest pair falls below acceptable separation. This is a focused local optimization around the current best conditions.

We have reached the maximum CRF, so use one more run to define the boundary of over-compression by shortening the gradient another step. This checks whether the optimum is broad or whether 16 min is the shortest fully acceptable method.

Since 16 min is optimal so far and 14 min over-compressed the critical pair, keep tG at 16 and slightly lower phi1 to soften the late gradient and test whether the 6/7 pair gains margin without sacrificing the zero time penalty. This probes whether the current optimum can be made more robust while staying at CRF 1.000.

The best method already reaches CRF 1.000, so a useful next check is temperature sensitivity around that optimum. A small increase in T may slightly change selectivity and either open the critical 6/7 pair or reveal that 40 C is already the best-balanced setting.

Higher temperature strongly collapsed the critical 6/7 pair, so test the opposite direction from the proven optimum. Lowering T may improve selectivity for that pair while staying near the same retention window, confirming whether 40 C is truly optimal.

Since increasing phi0 to 0.25 collapsed the front pair while 0.20 was optimal, test one step lower phi0 to see whether added early retention can preserve full resolution with a still-zero time penalty. This probes whether the optimum plateau extends toward slightly weaker starting conditions.

The optimum appears sharp in tG and robust only near 40 C, so test a slightly stronger final composition at the best phi0 and tG to see whether the last compound can be pulled a bit earlier without harming the critical mid-run separation. This is a small, targeted perturbation around the current maximum-CRF method.

The local optimum is already known, so use remaining runs to map selectivity around the critical cluster; lowering temperature another step may separate the problematic middle peaks differently than 35 C did. This helps confirm whether 40 C is uniquely favorable or whether a colder condition can produce an alternative high-resolution profile.

A slightly weaker starting composition may recover the critical mid-run spacing that was lost at 14 min while still keeping the method faster than the 16 min runs. This directly tests whether the time-optimal boundary can be shifted by compensating with lower phi0.

Lowering phi1 improved the critical pair at 16 min, so combine that softer endpoint with the faster 14 min gradient to see if the lost 6/7 separation can be recovered while preserving the shorter run. This is the most direct remaining route to challenge the 16 min optimum.

Both lowering phi0 and lowering phi1 individually helped recover some 6/7 separation at 14 min, so combine them to test whether their effects are additive. This is a targeted final check on whether a shorter-than-16 min method can still maintain full resolution.

This new composition pair achieved full resolution at 14 min, so the next step is to shorten the gradient again and see whether it can keep the critical 6/7 pair above threshold while preserving the zero time penalty. This directly tests whether an even faster member of this newly identified optimum region exists.

At 12 min the critical pair is too compressed, so weaken the starting composition one step to add early and mid-gradient retention while keeping the shorter gradient. This tests whether the 12 min method can be rescued by shifting compounds later without overly increasing the time term.

The 14 min, 0.15/0.85 method is tied for best with some margin on the critical pair, so test a slightly weaker final composition to see whether selectivity improves further while staying within the zero time-penalty region. This explores whether there is a more robust 14 min optimum around the same CRF ceiling.

The 0.15/0.85/14/40 method is tied for best, so probe its temperature sensitivity with a +5 C change. This checks whether the alternative optimum is more or less robust than the 0.20/0.90/16/40 method and whether selectivity around the critical pair improves or collapses.

The 14 min alternative optimum also degrades at higher temperature, so test 35 C to complete the local temperature map and confirm whether 40 C is the unique sweet spot for this composition. This can reveal whether the tied-best method is robust or highly temperature-specific.

The tied-best region at 14 min seems broad, and weakening both endpoints may further increase resolution margin while potentially remaining inside the zero time-penalty window. This is a targeted robustness test around the 0.15/0.85 optimum, especially for the critical 6/7 pair.

The 16 min optimum at phi0 0.20 had its main weakness in the 6/7 pair, while phi0 0.25 mostly affected the very front pair at a stronger endpoint; pairing phi0 0.25 with the softer phi1 0.85 may reveal a different selectivity balance. This is a worthwhile final unexplored neighborhood near the top-performing region.

With only a few runs left and the optimum already found, use them to probe a distinct selectivity perturbation in a fast regime that has not yet been temperature-tested. This can reveal whether a hotter, steeper condition reshuffles the critical cluster into a different separation pattern, even if it is unlikely to beat the current best.

A hotter temperature consistently hurts the known critical pair, but this composition has not yet been tested at 14 min and offers more retention margin than the hotter runs tried so far. With the optimum already secured, this is a final boundary-mapping experiment around temperature and endpoint strength.

For the last run, test the remaining untried corner adjacent to the successful 14 min region: weaker phi0 with stronger phi1 at 40 C. This completes the local map around the tied-best methods and checks whether that combination preserves full resolution with a favorable runtime.
